name: Beta-alanine
lead: Beta-alanine is a naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acid in which the amino group sits on the beta carbon (IUPAC name 3-aminopropanoic acid) [1]. It is the rate-limiting precursor of carnosine, a dipeptide stored at high concentration in skeletal muscle, where it acts as an intramuscular buffer [1]. As a supplement it is sold as a powder or capsule and is a staple ingredient of pre-workout formulas.

It is used mainly in efforts lasting roughly 0.5 to 10 minutes and in high-repetition training, on the reasoning that more carnosine buffers hydrogen ions and delays neuromuscular fatigue [1]. Its best-known acute effect is paraesthesia, a dose-dependent tingling sensation of the skin [1].

Meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials report small average benefits for exercise capacity, concentrated in efforts of about one to four minutes, with less consistent results for maximal-intensity and very short efforts [3][4]. It is not an agent that directly builds muscle tissue, and it is discussed in muscle-building communities chiefly as a performance and training-volume aid.
infobox: Glycine receptor agonist; GABA-A and GABA-C sites reported [1]

paras: Beta-alanine is taken by lifters, CrossFit-style athletes, rowers, runners and combat-sport athletes to support high-repetition sets and high-intensity intervals. Trials have tested it in high-intensity functional training, sport climbing, 10-km running time trials and multi-ingredient pre-workout products [8][9][10][15].
Because it does not directly add muscle, its place in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums is as an adjunct to training volume rather than an anabolic compound.

A 2023 narrative review assessed carnosine and beta-alanine supplementation in human medicine more broadly [12]. Registered trials have examined beta-alanine in adults with overweight or obesity and prediabetes (NCT05329610) and in cognition during a simulated military operation (NCT04250480) [21][22].

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 double-blind placebo-controlled studies (1,461 participants) concluded that beta-alanine supplementation has a small overall benefit for exercise measures [3]. A 2024 meta-analysis restricted to trained young men performing maximal or supramaximal efforts of 0.5 to 10 minutes (18 studies, 331 participants) found an overall effect size of 0.39 in favour of beta-alanine, with larger effects in efforts of 4 to 10 minutes [4].

A 2024 overview of sport supplements lists beta-alanine among a small set of supplements it covers [7]. Reviews of nutrition for female athletes have also considered it [5]. The International Society of Sports Nutrition has published a position stand on the supplement [14].

Individual studies report varied results. A multi-ingredient pre-workout study found that a blend containing beta-alanine and caffeine was compared with caffeine alone on bench press performance [8], and a study of acute pre-workout ingestion in basketball players tested a similar combination [13]. Because such products contain several active ingredients, the effect of beta-alanine alone cannot be isolated from them.

The only consistently reported adverse effect is paraesthesia, a tingling sensation that depends on dose [1]. Forum participants describe disliking this effect; one T Nation poster said they would prefer a beta-alanine-free version of a drink because of 'the tingles' [27]. Grokipedia states that splitting doses or using sustained-release forms reduces it, a claim attributed there to supplement research [2].

Wikipedia notes that no important adverse effects have been reported but that information on long-term use and on safety in combination with other supplements is lacking, and that many studies did not test supplement purity or for banned substances [1]. One forum user asked whether chronic supplementation could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism, citing a study on glucose uptake; the question was posed on T Nation without a published human study cited in support [25]. A registered trial examined 24 weeks of beta-alanine on muscle taurine and clinical blood parameters in healthy men (NCT03655041) [20].

Carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) occurs at about 17 to 25 mmol/kg dry muscle and contributes roughly 10 to 20 percent of buffering capacity in type I and II fibres; its imidazole group has a pKa near 6.8, suited to buffering [1]. Supplementing carnosine itself is less efficient because it is broken down into histidine and beta-alanine on digestion, so only about 40 percent of its weight is available as beta-alanine [1]. Human studies reported that oral beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine in the vastus lateralis and relates to high-intensity cycling capacity [18][19].

Beta-alanine is also a weak agonist at glycine receptors and has been reported to act at GABA-A, GABA-C and NMDA co-agonist sites, leading some authors to call it a putative small-molecule neurotransmitter [1].

It is formed endogenously from the breakdown of dihydrouracil and carnosine, can be transaminated with pyruvate, and is a component of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) and so of coenzyme A [1]. A review of histidine metabolism describes the carnosine pathway [6].

Industrially it is produced from ammonia and beta-propiolactone according to Wikipedia [1]; Grokipedia describes ammoniation of acrylic acid [2]. Its formula is C3H7NO2 and it lacks a stereocentre [1][2].

Beta-alanine appears in many commercial pre-workouts. On T Nation, the site's own products include formulas with 2 g and 3.5 g of beta-alanine per serving, and its marketing describes carnosine increases of up to 58 percent in four weeks and 80 percent in ten weeks [23][24][26]. A product developer on the forum said the company discussed dosing with a beta-alanine researcher and described a cumulative loading approach [28]. Customers discuss out-of-stock products and tingling in the same threads [29][27].

Human trials are numerous and mostly small. Meta-analyses: 40 studies in 2017 [3] and 18 studies in trained men in 2024 [4]. Randomised trials include a 4-week study in high-intensity functional training participants measuring neuromuscular fatigue [9], a study in sport climbers [10], an acute pre-workout study in well-trained basketball players [13], a pre-workout blend versus caffeine bench-press crossover [8], and a trial of a 10-km running time trial in active adults [15]. Another trial combined nutritional supplementation with aerobic exercise to look at brain systems [11].

Registered trials cover muscle carnosine (NCT00813553), aerobic-anaerobic transition performance in endurance athletes (NCT05096793), CrossFit performance (NCT05772988), high-intensity interval training (NCT03708185), heart rate response (NCT01745016), tennis players (NCT05427409) and simulated wrestling matches (NCT07641907) [30][31][32][33][34][35][36].

timeline.event: A study reports absorption of oral beta-alanine and its effect on carnosine synthesis in human vastus lateralis [18].
A study links beta-alanine supplementation, muscle carnosine and high-intensity cycling capacity [19].
International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on beta-alanine published [14].
Meta-analysis of 40 trials published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine [3].
Meta-analysis in trained young men reports an overall effect size of 0.39 [4].

lore.intro: Beta-alanine is discussed on T Nation mostly as one ingredient in pre-workouts, and 'the tingles' are a recurring topic of both fondness and complaint [27][25].

claims.claim: Beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine and so lets you do more work at high intensity
claims.believers: Product pages and forum posts state that carnosine rises by up to 58 percent in four weeks and 80 percent in ten weeks, which they say increases work that can be performed at high intensities [23].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report small but statistically significant benefits for exercise measures, strongest for efforts of 1 to 10 minutes [3][4].

claims.claim: The tingling is a sign it is working
claims.believers: Some users treat the tingles as confirmation that the product is active; others report disliking them [27].
claims.experts: Paraesthesia is a dose-dependent effect reported in the literature [1]; the sources do not link its intensity to performance effects.

claims.believers: Marketing for pre-workouts describes sustained power and rapid recovery between sets from beta-alanine [24][26].
claims.experts: The 2024 trained-male meta-analysis focused on efforts of 0.5 to 10 minutes [4]; Wikipedia limits support to 0.5 to 10 minute modalities [1]. A multi-ingredient bench-press study cannot isolate beta-alanine from the other ingredients [8].

claims.claim: Chronic use could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism or cause fatigue
claims.believers: A forum user raised this after reading a study on carnosine and glucose uptake [25].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that long-term safety data are lacking [1]; no human study cited here tests carnosine oversaturation.

claims.claim: Loading dose accumulation matters more than a single dose
claims.believers: A product developer described a cumulative loading process measured in grams over several weeks [28].
claims.experts: Studies describe raised carnosine after weeks of supplementation, with significant results at about four weeks in the 2024 analysis [4][18].
